description: Beyond Orbit is a team of curious minds passionate about space, science, and technology. We love exploring new ideas, solving problems, and turning our creativity into meaningful solutions. Through teamwork, research, and experimentation, we aim to tackle real-world challenges and learn along the way. We believe that great ideas begin with curiosity and that there's always something new to discover when we think beyond the ordinary.
summary:
AstroVoyage is a browser game where you design a real space mission. Pick a destination — the Moon, Mars or Jupiter — choose what you're going there to do, then build a spacecraft inside a real budget, mass, power and fuel limit. Launch it, and handle whatever goes wrong on the way.

Nothing in the flight is faked. The rocket equation, inverse-square sunlight, Hohmann transfers and launch windows are the real formulas; the planet data is JPL's and NSSDCA's. Every number on screen is marked as a NASA measurement, a real formula, or a game value we chose.

Two things take it past a simulation. Your finished mission exports as a real NASA GMAT script you can open and run in NASA's own software. And a Design Review checks your spacecraft the way Goddard's Mission Design Lab checks one, adding the contingency NASA actually requires — every percentage quoted from a 2012 Goddard paper.

It's built for students aged 12 and up, in plain English, because you can't learn trade-offs from a quiz. More power means more mass. More mass means more fuel. Something always has to give.
details:
You play the mission engineer. Pick a destination — Moon, Mars or Jupiter — and pick what you're actually going there to do: map the surface, hunt for water ice, watch dust storms, study Jupiter's magnetism. That goal decides which instrument you must carry, so it changes everything downstream.

Then you build the spacecraft from six part groups: bus, instruments, power, antenna, engine and launch rocket, plus how much fuel to load. Four live bars show money, mass, power and fuel as you choose. Six launch checks have to pass before you can fly — including whether you're even carrying the instrument your goal needs.

Next is the launch calendar, where the green months are real launch windows worked out from real orbital periods. Mars opens roughly every 26 months. Miss it and you wait.

Then you fly. A time-compressed simulation runs the cruise in about 60–90 seconds whatever the distance, with the scale always on screen ("Day 142 of 240 · 1 sec = 4 days"). You can watch it as a flat map or in 3D with three cameras — orbit, track, or follow behind the spacecraft. Challenges interrupt: a solar storm, a stuck antenna, a dust storm, a chance to grab bonus science. The game pauses and you choose. At Jupiter, with a 43-minute signal delay each way, you learn why real spacecraft have to look after themselves.

Finally you get a score, a star rating, a Flight Director write-up explaining what happened and why, and a comparison against the real missions that flew the same route — Chandrayaan-2, LRO, Mangalyaan, MAVEN, Juno.

How the physics works

Nothing in the flight is faked. Δv comes from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation with g₀ = 9.80665 m/s². Solar power falls off as inverse-square, which is why panels make 43% of Earth's power at Mars and 3.7% at Jupiter. Transfers are Hohmann half-ellipses timed with Kepler's equation, so the spacecraft genuinely moves fast near the Sun and slow far away. Signal delay is distance × 8.317 light-minutes per AU. Launch windows are derived from real synodic periods, not picked by hand.

All of it lives in pure TypeScript with no UI code in it, so every formula is unit-tested.

The two things we're proudest of

Your finished mission exports as a real NASA GMAT script — a .script file carrying your actual dry mass, propellant load, engine Isp, parking orbit and departure burn, in GMAT's own language. Open it in NASA's own mission design software and press Run. The game doesn't imitate mission design tools; it hands your mission to one.

And a NASA Design Review modelled on Goddard's Mission Design Lab. The launch checks ask "does it fit?" The review asks the harder question NASA asks: does it still fit once every subsystem adds the contingency it's required to add? Five subsystems each report CBE (current best estimate) → MEV (maximum expected value) against MPV (the hard limit). Every percentage is quoted — not estimated — from a 2012 NASA Goddard paper by Karpati, Hyde, Peabody and Garrison.

Benefits and intended impact

Space mission design is a chain of trade-offs you can't learn from a quiz. More power means more mass. More mass means more fuel. More fuel means a bigger rocket, which costs money you no longer have for instruments. The game makes you feel that chain instead of reading about it.

It's built for students aged 12 and up. Every message is short, plain English, and any jargon gets a one-line explanation. A 2–4 player team mode gives each player a real subsystem to own, so a classroom can argue about a design the way engineers actually do.

Tools

React 19, TypeScript and Vite, with state in zustand and tests in vitest. Plain CSS — no UI framework. The 3D views are our own renderer written from scratch in SVG and requestAnimationFrame: rotation, back-face culling, perspective projection, painter's-algorithm depth sorting and Lambert shading, all by hand. No 3D library. Sound is synthesised live in WebAudio from oscillators, so the game ships with no audio files. There's no backend and no API key — it's a static site, deployed on GitHub Pages.

How it's creative

A game that exports to professional engineering software is not a thing we'd seen. Nor is turning a NASA margin policy into a game mechanic: we took the paper's warning about "contingency pile-up" — every team padding a number that was already padded — and made it a number you have to manage.

The nicest accident: all three built-in designs pass the launch checks and fail the Design Review. Mars fails on dry mass, Jupiter on power. We left it that way, because both are real history — Mangalyaan flew on famously thin margins, and solar power at Jupiter is exactly why outer-planet missions carry nuclear batteries.

What we considered

Honesty first: every number is labelled as a real formula, a real NASA measurement, or a game value we chose, with a link for the first two. We'd rather say "we made this up to keep it fair" than quietly imply NASA said it.

Then accessibility and reach: it respects reduced-motion settings, is keyboard playable, keeps all text readable, fits a 1366×650 laptop with no scrolling, and stacks into one column on a phone.

And teaching over punishing: the Design Review is advisory, never blocking. A 12-year-old is always allowed to fly.

Quality is enforced, not hoped for: 485 unit tests, plus an automated check that plays a complete mission in a real browser and fails the build if the GMAT script is malformed or the review loses its sources.
